common_name: Rilona Amaryllis (Apricot-Salmon Amaryllis with Frilled Petals)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; prized for its unusual peachy apricot-salmon coloring, a shade uncommon among widely sold amaryllis cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Rilona bears large, frilly-edged apricot-salmon flowers up to 7 inches across with a pale brownish throat, a soft peachy tone that sets it apart from the more common solid reds and whites. Its tall, sturdy scapes make it a favorite for cut-flower use as well as container forcing, typically opening indoors in January and February. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground to naturalize, with foliage allowed to die back naturally each year to recharge the bulb.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Amputo is unusual among amaryllis for its pleasantly sweet fragrance and its trumpet-shaped pure white flowers with a green throat, a form that recalls a lily more than a typical broad-petaled amaryllis. It is somewhat more compact than large-flowered florist cultivars and has a reputation for tolerating brief cold snaps better than most Hippeastrum once established in the ground with winter mulch. Left in place in zone 8-10 gardens it naturalizes and returns to bloom each year.

common_name: Wedding Dance Amaryllis (Fully Double White Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; produces densely double, rose- or peony-like snow-white blooms, popular for indoor forcing and bridal-themed displays.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Wedding Dance produces large, densely double flowers built of many wavy, overlapping petals that give each bloom the multi-layered look of a rose or peony, snow-white with a faint creamy tint and soft green base. Multiple flowers typically open together on a single sturdy stem, creating an especially full, celebratory display well suited to holiday and event forcing indoors. Allow the foliage to grow on and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb for the following season.

common_name: Alfresco Amaryllis (Fully Double White Amaryllis with Chartreuse Throat)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; part of the Double Diamond Group, bred for reliable, fully double flowering with a lime-green throat.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Alfresco carries fully double, triple-layered pure-white blooms 5-6 inches across with a chartreuse throat set deep in the center of each flower, giving it a fuller, ruffled look than single-form cultivars. As a member of the Double Diamond Group it was bred specifically for consistent, reliable double flowering rather than the occasional stray single bloom seen in some older doubles. It performs well both as a container plant forced indoors for winter bloom and, in zone 8-10 gardens, as a naturalized perennial.

common_name: Elvas Amaryllis (White Amaryllis with Pink Picotee Edge)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; a peony-form double amaryllis noted for its pure white petals edged in deep pink-to-red picotee.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Elvas produces voluminous, peony-like double flowers packed with as many as 15 ruffled tepals, pure white with delicate pink-to-red picotee edges and fine raspberry brushmarks near the base of each petal. The waterlily-like blooms open 2-4 per stem and are large and long-lasting, making the cultivar a favorite both as a potted holiday bulb and as a cut flower. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be grown outdoors as a naturalizing perennial.

common_name: Terra Mystica Amaryllis (Terracotta-Pink Amaryllis with Plum Throat)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; a Diamond Group cultivar valued for an unusual terracotta-pink flower color with a dark plum throat.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Terra Mystica bears flared, 4-5 inch flowers in a distinctive terracotta-pink shade, each with a contrasting dark plum throat and a thin white picotee line tracing the petal edges as if hand-painted. Each bulb commonly sends up several stems with multiple flowers apiece, extending bloom over weeks when forced indoors. The unusual earthy coloring makes it a standout alongside the more familiar reds and whites of classic amaryllis cultivars.

common_name: Grand Diva Amaryllis (Dark Burgundy-Red Double Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; bears large, fully double flowers in a rich, dark burgundy-red.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Grand Diva produces large, fully double flowers in a deep burgundy-red that intensifies to an even richer, darker hue at the throat, giving the bloom noticeable depth compared with flatter, more uniformly colored cultivars. It performs well both as a forced container bulb for winter and holiday bloom and as a cut flower. In zone 8-10 gardens the bulbs can be left in place to naturalize as a permanent perennial.

common_name: Green Goddess Amaryllis (Dainty White Amaryllis with Green Center)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; bears smaller, more dainty white flowers with green centers than most large-flowered amaryllis.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Green Goddess bears white, lily-like flowers with soft green centers that are noticeably smaller and more delicate than the blooms of most large-flowered amaryllis hybrids, giving the plant a more graceful, refined look. It is a reliable choice for indoor winter forcing and can be moved outdoors once temperatures stay above about 65F. In zone 8-10 gardens it can also be grown in the ground as a naturalizing perennial bulb.

common_name: Red Pearl Amaryllis (Velvety Deep Crimson-Red Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; one of the darkest amaryllis cultivars, with intense velvety crimson-red flowers and an even darker throat.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Red Pearl bears large, velvety, deep crimson-red flowers up to 6 inches across with an even darker throat, and close inspection reveals fine striping in shades of wine, berry, and mahogany across each petal. It is regarded as one of the darkest-colored amaryllis cultivars commonly available, a dramatic contrast to brighter true-red types. It forces reliably indoors for winter bloom and can also be grown as a naturalizing perennial in zone 8-10 gardens.

common_name: Sonatini Balentino Amaryllis (Dwarf Hardy Scarlet Garden Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs outdoors after danger of frost has passed; part of the Sonatini Series, a group of compact garden amaryllis bred to be considerably more cold-tolerant than typical florist Hippeastrum, reported hardy into zone 7 with winter mulch.

directions: Sonatini Balentino is a compact, clump-forming garden amaryllis bearing scarlet-red flowers with a crisp white stripe down the center of each petal, smaller than large-flowered indoor cultivars but produced more abundantly, with up to four flower stems per bulb and several blooms per stem. Bred as part of the Sonatini Series specifically for outdoor planting, it is notably more cold-tolerant than typical florist Hippeastrum and can be left in the ground through mild winters where other amaryllis would need to be lifted. Left undisturbed it bulks up into an increasingly full flowering clump over successive summers, making it well suited to patio containers and sunny mixed borders rather than the classic indoor holiday-forcing role.
